description:
McDermott's Castle, also known as MacDermot's Castle and Castle Island, stands on a small island of about 0.23 ha in the south-east corner of Lough Key, in County Roscommon, and is National Monument no. 586. The Mac Diarmada (MacDermot) kings of Moylurg (Magh Luirg), in north-east Connacht, held the island as their seat between the 10th and 16th centuries, and there has been a fortification here since at least the 12th century.

In the early 19th century, when the castle was already a ruin, the architect John Nash remodelled it as a summer house or folly for the King family of the Rockingham estate. The battlements seen today date from then, and a late-medieval tower survives inside; the summer house itself burned in the mid-20th century. Excavations in 2019 found 13th-century buildings and high-status Gaelic objects, including silver pins and a gaming piece.

The island is private and there is no public landing. It can be seen from the water on the public boat tour run by Lough Key Boats from the Forest Park harbour, or from the shore of Lough Key Forest Park. The same boat passes Trinity Island, where Holy Trinity Abbey stands, and the legend of Úna Bhán is told on board.
history:
The Mac Diarmada (MacDermot) kings of Moylurg (Magh Luirg), in north-east Connacht, made Castle Island their seat between the 10th and 16th centuries, and there has been a fortification on the island since at least the 12th century. In 1184 the Annals of Loch Cé record that lightning burned “the Rock of Loch Cé”, the royal residence, with great loss of life. In 1235 a rebuilt castle was besieged during Richard Mór de Burgh's conquest of Connacht, first with a catapult mounted on a raft and then with fire ships, and Cormac MacDermot, king of Moylurg, had to surrender. The MacDermots lost the island in 1586.

In the early 19th century, when it was already in ruins, the island was remodelled by the architect John Nash as a summer house or folly for the King family of the Rockingham estate. The present battlements are from that time, around a late-medieval tower, and the summer house burned in the mid-20th century. The island appeared in the sitcom Moone Boy in 2014. In 2018 it was offered for sale at around €80,000, but the sale was withdrawn and the island remains in private hands. Excavations in 2019 found 13th-century buildings and high-status Gaelic objects.

The story goes that Úna Bhán MacDermot, daughter of Brian Óg MacDermot (king of Moylurg 1603–36), could not marry Tomás Láidir Costello, the son of an enemy of her father. She died of grief and was buried on Trinity Island, and Tomás is said to have swum to her grave and later to have been buried beside her. This is a 17th-century legend, and the grave is on Trinity Island, at Holy Trinity Abbey, not on Castle Island.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Lough Key Forest Park is 3 km east of Boyle town on the N61. Boyle is accessible by train from Dublin (via Mullingar, approximately 2 hours) or by bus from Galway and Sligo. A car is the most practical option for reaching the lake from the nearest train station.

**Seeing the castle:** The island is private and there is no public landing. You can see it from the water on the public boat tour run by Lough Key Boats from the Forest Park harbour, 3 km east of Boyle, or from the shore of Lough Key Forest Park. The tour uses a covered, heated boat, The Trinity, with 40 seats; it lasts 1 hour and passes Trinity Island, Church Island and Castle Island. On the 2026 timetable it runs on weekends in May, June and September at 13:30 and 15:00, and daily in July and August at 13:30, 15:00 and 16:30. Adults pay €22, children €10 and seniors and students €18, and children under 3 go free. Private boat trips and rowing-boat hire are also available. Check current times with the operator, and contact the operator outside the season.

**Practical tips:** Lough Key Forest Park has woodland trails, a canopy walk and a bog garden, and the castle is visible across the water from several points on the shoreline path; the Forest Park has a separate entrance fee.

**Combine with:** Lough Key Forest Park and Boyle town are the base for the visit. Castle hotels nearby include [Kilronan Castle](/castles/ireland/kilronan-castle), about 9 km to the north, [Markree Castle](/castles/ireland/markree-castle), about 25 km to the north-west, and [Lough Rynn Castle](/castles/ireland/lough-rynn-castle), about 27 km to the south-east.

faqs.question: Can you visit McDermott's Castle?
faqs.answer: No. The island is private and there is no public landing, so you cannot walk around the castle. You can see it from the water on the public boat tour from the Forest Park harbour, or from the shore of Lough Key Forest Park. Do not try to land from a private boat.

faqs.question: How much is the Lough Key boat tour and when does it run?
faqs.answer: The public boat tour run by Lough Key Boats from the Forest Park harbour lasts 1 hour. Adults pay €22, children €10 and seniors and students €18, and children under 3 go free. On the 2026 timetable it runs on weekends in May, June and September at 13:30 and 15:00, and daily in July and August at 13:30, 15:00 and 16:30. Check current times with the operator, and contact the operator outside the season.

faqs.question: When was McDermott's Castle built?
faqs.answer: There has been a fortification on the island since at least the 12th century, and the Annals of Loch Cé record the royal residence there burned by lightning in 1184. The shell seen today is mostly an early-19th-century folly: John Nash remodelled the ruin as a summer house for the King family of Rockingham, around a late-medieval tower.

faqs.question: Who owns McDermott's Castle?
faqs.answer: It is privately owned. The MacDermots lost the island in 1586, and in 2018 it was offered for sale at around €80,000; the sale was withdrawn and the island remains in private hands.

faqs.answer: The story goes that Úna Bhán MacDermot, daughter of Brian Óg MacDermot, king of Moylurg from 1603 to 1636, could not marry Tomás Láidir Costello, the son of an enemy of her father. She died of grief and was buried on Trinity Island, and Tomás is said to have swum to her grave and later to have been buried beside her. It is a 17th-century legend, and the grave is on Trinity Island, at Holy Trinity Abbey, not on Castle Island.
